title: Quantifying Differences Between Floodplain Waterbody Connectivity and River‐Floodplain Connectivity in a Coastal Meandering River
content:
Abstract

Riparian landscapes support biodiverse and productive ecosystems that in turn provide valuable services like water filtration and flood attenuation. Extensive anthropogenic modifications to riparian environments have altered natural water connectivity patterns important for ecosystem health, leading to an increased effort to understand and restore natural floodplain connectivity. It is well known that secondary floodplain channels facilitate exchange at the river-floodplain boundary with increasing discharge, but comparatively little is known about connectivity of floodplain waterbodies that are productivity hotspots in riparian ecosystems. In this study we investigate patterns of floodplain and floodplain waterbody connectivity in the coastal meandering Mission River, TX, USA. We use a modeling approach to examine water movement and connectivity, and find that water exchange generally increases with discharge, while the number of active floodplain connections is greatest at moderate flows. We also observe that the number of effective connections, a measure of connection prominence, is maximized at moderate discharges and is typically one-third to half the number of active connections, indicating that few connections dominate river-floodplain exchange. Counterintuitively, we find that exchange at the river-floodplain interface is most uneven at the highest discharges, despite complete bank inundation. We interpret a process-based transition in connectivity from being topographically controlled at lower discharges to hydraulically controlled at high discharges, and identify a spatial association to this transition. Finally, we consider that exchange and exposure time in each floodplain region can describe nutrient processing potential in a framework that reflects complexity inherent in natural floodplains.
